lessons.title: The Arabs and thE Rise of Islam

cards.title: The Arabs and thE Rise of Islam
body: Arabs- are Semitic speaking people of the Arabian Peninsula who led a nomadic life by moving around the desert for food and water organized into tribes ruled by sheiks. The sheiks were chosen by the Mejlis (council of elders).
The early Arabs were involved in farming, herding and caravan trade (land trade). They were polytheistic and traced their ancestry to Abraham and his son Ishmael.

The political disorders in Mesopotamia, Byzantine and Persia resulted in the shift of trade from the old route to a new route that passed by Yemen and the Indian Ocean, thus increased the importance of the Arabian Peninsula. Cities like Mecca benefited from the new trade routes creating a gap between the rich and poor.

cards.title: The Life of Mohammad
body: Mohammad was born in Mecca in 570 C.E and worked in trade after marrying Khadija. He was worried about the growing gap between the rich and the poor thus used to meditate. He received revelations from God through an angel that were later written in the Quran.

His teachings of Islam (submission to the will of Allah) in Mecca were rejected by the Qurayesh (wealthy tribe) who begun persecuting his followers. Some of his followers came to the Red Sea to gain refuge from the Aksumite king.

In 622, Mohammed fled into Medina (city of the prophet) in what is known as the Hijrah and formed the first Islamic community known as the Umma in Medina where he was both the political and religious leader. He returned to Mecca in 630 and preached Islam until his death after 2 years.

cards.title: The Teachings of Mohammad
body: Islam is a monotheistic religion like Christianity and Judaism and believes Mohammad to be the last prophet. It stresses on obeying Allah through the 5 pillars of Islam;
1. Shahadah- belief in one God, Allah and his messenger Mohammad
2. Salaat- to pray 5 times a day
3. Zakat- giving a percentage of one’s wealth to the poor
4. Sawm- fasting during Ramadan (holy month)
5. Hajj- pilgrimage to Mecca at least once in a lifetime to the Kaaba
The Shariah is the Muslim law-code created by the Muslim scholars known as the Ulama after Mohammad’s death.

cards.title: Completing this point: the Five Pillars and the Shariah
body: **The Five Pillars are the five basic duties of every Muslim.** 1) **Shahadah** – declaring faith in one God, Allah, and Mohammad as his messenger; 2) **Salat** – praying five times a day facing Mecca; 3) **Zakat** – giving a share of one's wealth to the poor; 4) **Sawm** – fasting from dawn to sunset in **Ramadan**; 5) **Hajj** – the pilgrimage to the Kaaba in Mecca at least once in a lifetime, if able.

**The Shariah.** After Mohammad's death, scholars (the **Ulama**) developed the Shariah, the Islamic law code, from the Quran and the sayings and practice of the Prophet (the Hadith and Sunna). It guides daily life, family matters and trade.
**Memory trick – "Say, Pray, Pay, Fast, Go":** Shahadah, Salat, Zakat, Sawm, Hajj.

cards.title: Model answer: the Hijrah
cards.problem: (Exam question) What was the Hijrah and why is it important?

steps.text: Background: Mohammed's teaching of Islam in Mecca was rejected by the wealthy Qurayesh, who persecuted his followers (some found refuge with the Aksumite king).
Event: in 622 Mohammed fled from Mecca to Medina – the Hijrah.
Result: in Medina he formed the first Islamic community, the Umma, and was both its political and religious leader.
Importance: the Muslim (Hejira) calendar starts from it; in 630 he returned to Mecca.

cards.answer: The Hijrah was Mohammed's flight from Mecca to Medina in 622, where he founded the Umma; it marks the start of the Islamic calendar.

cards.title: The Appearance of Islamic Empires
body: In 632, one of Mohammad’s closest followers, Abu Baker, became a Caliph (the successor of Mohammad). The Islamic movement grew towards the Byzantine Empire by defeating them at Yamruk in 636, Syria (640), Egypt and North Africa (642) and the Persian Empire in 650. Islamic expansion was successful because;
1. Both the Byzantine and Persia were weakened due to constant wars
2. The locals were dissatisfied with Imperial rule and accepted the new Arab regime
3. The Muslim fighters were motivated because believed that fighting and dying would fulfilling their religious duties
4. Each newly conquered land was secured by moving large Arab populations to it
In 750 C.E, the center of Islamic rule shifted from Medina to Damascus with the rise of the Umayyad dynasty.

cards.title: Completing this point: why Islam expanded so fast
body: **Reason 1 – weak neighbours.** The Byzantine and Persian empires had exhausted each other in long wars.

**Reason 2 – welcome from local people.** Many subjects resented high imperial taxes and religious persecution and accepted the new Arab rulers, who often allowed Christians and Jews to keep their faith in return for a tax.
**Reason 3 – religious motivation.** Muslim fighters believed that fighting for the faith was a religious duty.
**Reason 4 – settlement.** Arab populations were moved into conquered lands to secure them.
**Key dates.** Yarmuk 636, Syria 640, Egypt 642, Persia about 650. The Umayyads moved the capital from Medina to **Damascus** (661); the Abbasids later built **Baghdad** (750 onwards).
**Memory trick:** "Weak – Welcome – Willing – Settled."

cards.title: 1) The Umayyad Dynasty (661-750)
body: Abu Baker was succeeded by Caliph Omer, who was in return succeeded by Caliph Osman. Many Muslims weren’t satisfied with Osman because they wanted Ali (Mohammad’s cousin) to be the Caliph, Osman was assassinated in 656 and was succeeded by Ali. Caliph Ali was also assassinated by the Mu’awiyahs (Syria’s governors).

In 661, Amir Mu’awiyah became the Caliph and established the Umayyad Dynasty with Damascus as his capital, they converted the Berbers (North African natives) into Islam and conquered Spain (710) with its center at Cordoba, Mesopotamia and central Asia. They failed in Byzantine and France (717 &732) after losing the Battle of Tours (Gaul, France).
Decline- 1. Internal crisis as the non-Arab Muslims (Byzantines &Persians) were being ignored by the rulers.
2. Ali’s second son, Hussein, led a revolt against the Umayyads resulting in the split of Muslims into Shiite and Sunni.

The Shiites (a minority found in Iran and Iraq) accepted only the descendants of Ali as the Caliphs while the Sunnis (a majority found all over the world) believed that any Muslim including the Umayyads could be Caliphs.

cards.title: 2) The Abbasid Dynasty (750-1258)
body: 750, Abu al-Abbas, a descendant of Mohammad, set up the Abbasid by overthrowing the Umayyads with its capital at Baghdad (Iraq). They benefited from river and caravan trade in the Persian Gulf and the Mediterranean region.

The society was composed of Arabs and non-Arabs who had equal civil and military rights. The dynasty reached its height under Harun al-Rashid who supported artists, writers and learning. The dynasty conquered provinces of the Roman Empire and trade routes to the East.
Decline- 1. Wars of succession
2. Financial Corruption
3. Shortage of qualified Arabs in key positions Arabs led to non-Arab domination as they began to rule provinces and broke away from the central government.

cards.title: 3) The Seljuk Turks
body: Were nomadic Turkish soliders from central Asia who converted into Islam after being hired by the Fatimids of Egypt under the Abbasid dynasty.

The Seljuks grew stronger after the fall of the Abbasids and expanded into Iran, Armenia, Baghdad (1055) and Byzantine (1071). Their invasion of the Byzantine Empire made the Emperor (Alexis I) ask for European help leading to the Crusades

cards.title: 4) The Mongols
body: Were non-Muslim Pastoral people from the Gobi desert who controlled mush of Asia including Persia and Mesopotamia by defeating the Baghdad Caliphate (1258) under their leader Genghis Khan. The Mongols were violent, they burned cities and destroyed villages.
Their attempts to control Egypt failed because of strong resistance from the Mamluks (Turkish slave-soldiers ruling Egypt). The Mongols eventually began to intermarry with locals and grew in numbers.

cards.title: Islamic Civilizations
body: All Islamic Civilizations had similar characteristics such as;

cards.title: Completing this point: common features of Islamic civilizations
body: **1. Extensive trade.** Arab merchants traded by ship and camel caravan with China (silk, porcelain), India and Southeast Asia (spices, sandalwood), Africa (gold, ivory, slaves) and the Byzantine Empire. Banking and coins made exchange easier.
**2. Great cities.** Baghdad (the "City of Peace") under the Abbasids, Cairo under the Fatimids, and Damascus. Each city had palaces, a great mosque, public baths and a covered market (**bazaar**).

**3. A class society.** In theory all are equal before Allah, but in practice there was an upper class (rulers, officials, rich merchants) and a lower class. Slavery existed, but freeing slaves was considered a good act.
**4. Rights for women.** Women could own and inherit property and had some right to divorce, although men were dominant.

**5. Rich culture and learning.** Muslim scholars preserved and translated Greek works and made advances in mathematics (algebra, Arabic numerals), astronomy, medicine and philosophy. Architecture featured mosques with domes and minarets and geometric decoration.
**Memory trick:** "T-C-S-W-L: Trade, Cities, Society, Women, Learning."

cards.title: 1) Trade and Cities
body: Caravan and sea trade were conducted with the whole world. Trade was highly simplified by the development of banking and coinage systems and it gave rise to rich cities such as Baghdad, Cairo under the Fatimids and Damascus.
Each city had public buildings with fountains, public baths, bazzars (marketplaces) and great Mosques while in the country sides, people lived off farming and herding.

cards.title: 2) Society
body: Even though Islam considered all people as equals and prohibits Slavery, the Islamic society was divided into upper class (rulers, senior officials and wealthy merchants) and lower class (the rest of the society). Non-Muslim slaves were bought from Africa and Asia to serve in the army and domestic works. The slaves were allowed to buy their own freedom.
In the Quran, Women had the right to own and inherit property but were subjected to male guardians who dictated their marriages while men could have 4 wives. Adultery was forbidden to all.

cards.title: 3) Culture
body: Muslim Arabs absorbed the Greco-Roman culture; they translated the books of Plato and Aristotle into Arabic and kept them in the House of Wisdom (Library in Baghdad). They brought Mathematics from India and Paper from China.

cards.title: 4) Philosophy, Science and History
body: Philosophy developed under Muslim philosophers such as Ibn-Rashid, while mathematics and numerical system were adapted from India. Al Khwarizmi was a famous mathematician who shaped Algebra in the 9th C.

An Observatory was set up in Baghdad and it was used in Astronomy. Ibn Sina was the scientist who wrote the medical Encyclopedia. Ibn-Khaldun was a famous historian, he wrote Introduction to History in the 14th C.

cards.title: 5) Islamic Literature, Art and Architecture
body: The greatest literary works include the Quran, the Rubaiyat written by Omer Khayyam and The Thousand and One nights (Arabian nights). Islamic art is a combination of Arab, Turkish and Persian traditions; they built great palaces and mosques such as the Great Mosque of Samarra (Iran), the mosque of Cordoba (southern Spain) and large brick castles in Syria.
Islamic art doesn’t contain any imitations of God or living beings thus, geometric figures were used.
